title: Leveraging contact network structure in the design of cluster randomized trials
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design cluster randomized trials in settings where intervention effects are affected by contact network structure, especially infectious disease outbreaks. The core question is whether trial designs can both preserve statistical power and improve public health impact by ordering cluster enrollment or vaccination according to how connected clusters are to one another.

The authors propose a family of connectivity-informed cluster randomized trial designs, including Static Rank and Adaptive Rank variants, along with Fuzzy Order, Holdback, and Ranked Parallel options. These designs use baseline or updated between-cluster connectivity to determine which clusters are vaccinated earlier, with the aim of reducing cross-cluster transmission while still allowing randomized comparisons in some variants. The paper evaluates these designs through simulation rather than a real-world educational intervention.

The simulated context is an Ebola-like epidemic on a network-structured population, with clusters of individuals connected by within- and between-cluster ties. Using agent-based epidemic simulations, the authors compare epidemic outcomes and statistical power across standard Parallel and Stepped Wedge cluster trial designs versus connectivity-informed alternatives. They find that connectivity-informed designs can reduce cumulative incidence and peak infectiousness, but usually lower power to detect vaccine effects; adding a brief holdback period recovers much of that lost power.

Overall, the paper concludes that incorporating network connectivity into CRT design can improve outbreak control with modest trade-offs in inferential power. It is presented as a methodological contribution for infectious disease trials and broader spreading-process interventions, not as an educational or ChatGPT-tutoring study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological simulation paper about cluster randomized trial design, not an empirical study of an educational or AI intervention. It does not evaluate learner outcomes in education, so it does not meet criteria for an evidence tier in the K-12 intervention framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact and no student outcome effects are estimated. Its contribution is methodological for infectious disease trial design, so there is no measurable educational impact to classify.
